newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says 2,000 killed in Rwandan army sweeps.
newsitem.headline: UN says 2,000 killed in Rwandan army sweeps.

text.p: The U.N. human rights office said on Friday that more than 2,000 mostly unarmed civilians had been killed in Rwanda during army sweeps in May and June and urged the government to put an end to the excessive use of force by troops.

In a report in Geneva, the office said at least 2,022 people had been killed during military operations in May and June in Ruhengeri, a predominantly Hutu northwestern region where the Tutsi-dominated army is fighting a rebellion.
It expressed alarm at Rwandan Patriotic Army (RPA) operations in Ruhengeri in response to rebel attacks that resulted in the deaths of civilians including many elderly people, women and children.
It asked the government, dominated by minority Tutsis who took power after 1994's genocide of half a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates, to halt the army's excessive use of force.
"The government of Rwanda should take steps to prevent the excessive use of force by the security forces, including the RPA," it said.
The killings were a record high for any two-month reporting period, the report said.
In one tiny village, Nkuli, it said RPA troops killed a total of 1,226 people alone in a cordon-and-search operation between May 9 and 12 following a rebel attack on an army convoy.

Soldiers searched houses and fatally shot or stabbed people they suspected of aiding the rebels, it said. "According to reports collected from eyewitnesses, the majority of those killed were children and elderly persons," it added.
Of these victims, 404 were from the area of Ryinyo, 325 from Gitwa, 253 from Mukamira, 146 from Gatovu and 98 from Rukoma -- tiny rural settlements in far-flung hills of northwest Rwanda.

The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said it was aware of the killings in the mountainous region on Zaire's frontier where Western aid workers pulled out after a series of brutal and unexplained murders of expatriate staff earlier this year.
"We know there are many killings taking place. We know there is major fighting going on. We don't have the presence we'd like in many of these areas," said UNHCR spokeswoman Pam O'Toole.

Agencies suspended work by local staff in Ruhengeri in June after the murders of a Hutu UNHCR driver and his family and two Hutu World Food Programme employees, one arrested by troops and the other questioned by soldiers prior to their deaths.
On Thursday, Amnesty International accused the world of ignoring the slaughter of more than 2,300 unarmed Rwandan civilians in May, June and July.
The London-based human rights group said among the victims were Rwandan Hutu refugees who returned after their camps in former Zaire were attacked by rebels backed by Rwanda.
